displayText: White always moves first. After that, the players take turns, one move each.
text: White always moves first. After that, the players take turns, one move each.

displayText: The rook attacks straight up the open column to the black king. The knight and the bishop cannot reach the king's square.
text: The rook attacks straight up the open column to the black king. The knight and the bishop cannot reach the king's square.

displayText: f6 is where the f-file meets the sixth rank: go along to the f-file, then count up six. The white knight stands there.
text: F six is where the f-file meets the sixth rank: go along to the f-file, then count up six. The white knight stands there.

displayText: The files run from a on White's left to h on White's right, and White's nearest rank is 1, so the right-hand corner is h1. It is a light square.
text: The files run from a on White's left to h on White's right, and White's nearest rank is 1, so the right-hand corner is H one. It is a light square.

displayText: The pawn can step to d3, or make its double step to d4 because both squares are empty. It can also capture diagonally forward: the knight on c3 or the bishop on e3. The rook on f4 is out of its reach.
text: The pawn can step to D three, or make its double step to D four because both squares are empty. It can also capture diagonally forward: the knight on C three or the bishop on E three. The rook on F four is out of its reach.

displayText: The pawn on c5 attacks b6 and d6, and the pawn on g4 attacks f5 and h5. The pieces straight ahead on c6 and g5 only block the pawns, and the bishop on f3 is behind the pawn on g4.
text: The pawn on C five attacks B six and D six, and the pawn on G four attacks F five and H five. The pieces straight ahead on C six and G five only block the pawns, and the bishop on F three is behind the pawn on G four.

displayText: Reaching the far rank wins Pawn Duel at once. Pawns never promote in this game.
text: Reaching the far rank wins Pawn Duel at once. Pawns never promote in this game.

displayText: The pawn on c4 can take on b5 or d5, the pawn on e4 can also take on d5, and the pawn on f3 can take on g4. The pawn on e5 is straight in front of a white pawn, so it cannot be captured.
text: The pawn on C four can take on B five or D five, the pawn on E four can also take on D five, and the pawn on F three can take on G four. The pawn on E five is straight in front of a white pawn, so it cannot be captured.

displayText: The rook moves along the e-file and the fourth rank. Its own pawn on e7 stops it at e6. It can capture the knight on b4 and the pawn on g4, but cannot go past them.
text: The rook moves along the e-file and the fourth rank. Its own pawn on E seven stops it at E six. It can capture the knight on B four and the pawn on G four, but cannot go past them.

displayText: The rook slides along the third rank and takes Black's rook on a3, where nothing can capture it back. Taking the pawn on d6 would lose the rook to the pawn on e7.
text: The rook slides along the third rank and takes Black's rook on A three, where nothing can capture it back. Taking the pawn on D six would lose the rook to the pawn on E seven.

displayText: Up the d-file the rook reaches the pawn on d7, and along the fourth rank it reaches the pawn on a4. White's own pawn on f4 shields the pawn on h4.
text: Up the d-file the rook reaches the pawn on D seven, and along the fourth rank it reaches the pawn on A four. White's own pawn on F four shields the pawn on H four.

displayText: In Rook Sweep the pawns never move. Each side moves its rook to capture the opposing pawns.
text: In Rook Sweep the pawns never move. Each side moves its rook to capture the opposing pawns.

displayText: The bishop moves along its four diagonals. Its own pawn on d6 stops it at e5, and it can capture the rook on h6 and the knight on c1.
text: The bishop moves along its four diagonals. Its own pawn on D six stops it at E five, and it can capture the rook on H six and the knight on C one.

displayText: From d5 the bishop attacks the rook on b7 and the rook on f3, in opposite directions along the same long diagonal. Neither rook can capture the bishop, and Black can move only one of them.
text: From D five the bishop attacks the rook on B seven and the rook on F three, in opposite directions along the same long diagonal. Neither rook can capture the bishop, and Black can move only one of them.

displayText: The dark-squared bishop on c3 can take the pawn on b4, which shields the pawn on a5. The light-squared bishop on e2 can take the pawn on g4 through the empty f3 square.
text: The dark-squared bishop on C three can take the pawn on B four, which shields the pawn on A five. The light-squared bishop on E two can take the pawn on G four through the empty F three square.

displayText: Each bishop keeps its square colour. White's light-squared bishop can never reach the black pawns or Black's bishop, which all stand on dark squares, and Black's dark-squared bishop can never reach the white pawn or White's bishop, which stand on light squares. No remaining target can be reached, so the game is a draw.
text: Each bishop keeps its square colour. White's light-squared bishop can never reach the black pawns or Black's bishop, which all stand on dark squares, and Black's dark-squared bishop can never reach the white pawn or White's bishop, which stand on light squares. No remaining target can be reached, so the game is a draw.

displayText: Along the c-file she stops before her pawn on c7. On the fourth rank she can capture the bishop on g4, and on the diagonals she can capture the knight on f7 and the pawn on a6. Towards e2 she can go only as far as d3, because her own pawn stands on e2.
text: Along the c-file she stops before her pawn on C seven. On the fourth rank she can capture the bishop on G four, and on the diagonals she can capture the knight on F seven and the pawn on A six. Towards E two she can go only as far as D three, because her own pawn stands on E two.

displayText: The queen captures the rook on a5, and no black piece can reach her there. Taking the knight on d6 would lose her to the pawn on e7.
text: The queen captures the rook on A five, and no black piece can reach her there. Taking the knight on D six would lose her to the pawn on E seven.

displayText: The pawns on a2, c2, g2 and h4 have no pawn guarding them. The pawn on b3 is protected by a2 and c2, f3 by g2, and e4 by f3.
text: The pawns on A two, C two, G two and H four have no pawn guarding them. The pawn on B three is protected by A two and C two, F three by G two, and E four by F three.

displayText: The queen attacks e3 down the file, and c3 and f4 along her diagonals. The pawns on b2 and h2 are on those diagonals too, but hidden behind c3 and f4.
text: The queen attacks E three down the file, and C three and F four along her diagonals. The pawns on B two and H two are on those diagonals too, but hidden behind C three and F four.

displayText: The knight jumps over the pawns beside it. It cannot land on its own pawns on e3 and c7, but it can capture the black pawn on f6.
text: The knight jumps over the pawns beside it. It cannot land on its own pawns on E three and C seven, but it can capture the black pawn on F six.

displayText: From c7 the knight attacks both the queen on e8 and the rook on a8. No black piece can capture it there, and Black cannot move both pieces away at once, so White wins material.
text: From C seven the knight attacks both the queen on E eight and the rook on A eight. No black piece can capture it there, and Black cannot move both pieces away at once, so White wins material.

displayText: From c6 the knight can jump to a5, taking the pawn, or to e7, taking the bishop.
text: From C six the knight can jump to A five, taking the pawn, or to E seven, taking the bishop.

displayText: Black pawns capture diagonally towards rank 1, so the pawn on e5 covers d4 and f4. The knight may not land on either.
text: Black pawns capture diagonally towards rank 1, so the pawn on E five covers D four and F four. The knight may not land on either.

displayText: The rook on h1 attacks a1, b1 and c1, and a3, b3 and c3 touch the black king. Only a2 and c2 are safe.
text: The rook on H one attacks A one, B one and C one, and A three, B three and C three touch the black king. Only A two and C two are safe.

displayText: The king is beyond value. It is never captured, and if it is checkmated the game is over.
text: The king is beyond value. It is never captured, and if it is checkmated the game is over.

displayText: The rook's line along the fourth rank stops at the pawn on c4, and the bishop covers b4, so the king crosses at a4. From there b5, c6 and c7 lead safely to c8.
text: The rook's line along the fourth rank stops at the pawn on C four, and the bishop covers B four, so the king crosses at A four. From there B five, C six and C seven lead safely to C eight.

displayText: The rook covers c3, d3 and e3, the bishop covers c3 and c5, and the pawn on f5 attacks e4. That leaves c4, d5 and e5.
text: The rook covers C three, D three and E three, the bishop covers C three and C five, and the pawn on F five attacks E four. That leaves C four, D five and E five.

displayText: The rook checks along the eighth rank. The black king's own pawns block g7 and h7, and the rook covers g8, so there is no escape.
text: The rook checks along the eighth rank. The black king's own pawns block G seven and H seven, and the rook covers G eight, so there is no escape.

displayText: The king cannot move: f1 and h1 are both on the rook's rank. Nothing can block on f1, but the knight on d3 can capture the rook on e1.
text: The king cannot move: F one and H one are both on the rook's rank. Nothing can block on F one, but the knight on D three can capture the rook on E one.

displayText: White's queen begins on d1. That square is light, matching her colour, and the white king stands next to her on e1.
text: White's queen begins on D one. That square is light, matching her colour, and the white king stands next to her on E one.

displayText: From each corner the order is rook, knight, bishop, so Black's knights start on b8 and g8, right next to the rooks.
text: From each corner the order is rook, knight, bishop, so Black's knights start on B eight and G eight, right next to the rooks.

displayText: The king moves two squares from e1 to g1, and the rook jumps from h1 to f1.
text: The king moves two squares from E one to G one, and the rook jumps from H one to F one.

displayText: The king moves two squares from e1 to c1, and the rook jumps over it from a1 to d1.
text: The king moves two squares from E one to C one, and the rook jumps over it from A one to D one.

displayText: The bishop on b5 attacks f1, so the king cannot cross it to castle kingside. On the queenside d1 and c1 are safe, so White castles there.
text: The bishop on B five attacks F one, so the king cannot cross it to castle kingside. On the queenside D one and C one are safe, so White castles there.

displayText: The king must not start, cross or land on an attacked square. It never touches b1, so an attack on b1 does not matter.
text: The king must not start, cross or land on an attacked square. It never touches B one, so an attack on B one does not matter.

displayText: The pawn on e7 steps to e8, where it can become a queen. The pawn on b6 still needs two more moves.
text: The pawn on E seven steps to E eight, where it can become a queen. The pawn on B six still needs two more moves.

displayText: The pawn on d5 captures en passant by moving to c6, and the black pawn on c5 is removed. From c6 the pawn attacks the king on b7. This capture is only allowed straight after Black's double step.
text: The pawn on D five captures en passant by moving to C six, and the black pawn on C five is removed. From C six the pawn attacks the king on B seven. This capture is only allowed straight after Black's double step.

displayText: The queen on d8 or f8 checks the king along the back rank, and the white king covers a7 and b7. Moving the queen to c7 instead would leave Black with no legal move: stalemate.
text: The queen on D eight or F eight checks the king along the back rank, and the white king covers A seven and B seven. Moving the queen to C seven instead would leave Black with no legal move: stalemate.

displayText: Black's king on h1 is not in check, but White's king covers g1 and g2 and the knight covers h2. Black has no legal move, so it is stalemate and the game is drawn.
text: Black's king on H one is not in check, but White's king covers G one and G two and the knight covers H two. Black has no legal move, so it is stalemate and the game is drawn.

displayText: A knight (3) and a bishop (3) make 6 points. A rook (5) and a pawn (1) also make 6. A queen is 9, and two pawns only 2.
text: A knight (3) and a bishop (3) make 6 points. A rook (5) and a pawn (1) also make 6. A queen is 9, and two pawns only 2.

displayText: The rook on a7 is worth five points and nothing guards it. Taking the pawn on d5 or g7 would cost the queen, worth nine, for one point.
text: The rook on A seven is worth five points and nothing guards it. Taking the pawn on D five or G seven would cost the queen, worth nine, for one point.

displayText: The knight on f3, the rook on e1 and the pawn on d4 all attack e5. The bishop on c1 and the queen on d1 do not reach it.
text: The knight on F three, the rook on E one and the pawn on D four all attack E five. The bishop on C one and the queen on D one do not reach it.

displayText: The rook on a8, the knight on c6, the bishop on d6 and the pawn on b5 have no defender. The rook guards the pawn on a7, and the king guards f7, g7 and h7.
text: The rook on A eight, the knight on C six, the bishop on D six and the pawn on B five have no defender. The rook guards the pawn on A seven, and the king guards F seven, G seven and H seven.

displayText: B is the bishop, x means a capture, and e5 is the square where the capture happens. A pawn capture would start with a small file letter, as in dxe5.
text: B is the bishop, x means a capture, and E five is the square where the capture happens. A pawn capture would start with a small file letter, as in dxe5.

displayText: R is the rook, d8 is its target square and # means checkmate. The rook on d8 checks along the back rank and also covers f8 and h8, while Black's own pawns on f7, g7 and h7 block the king's way forward.
text: R is the rook, D eight is its target square and # means checkmate. The rook on D eight checks along the back rank and also covers F eight and H eight, while Black's own pawns on F seven, G seven and H seven block the king's way forward.

displayText: Touch-move: a piece of your own that you touch on purpose must be moved if it can move legally. Announcing an adjustment works only before touching, and only to straighten a piece.
text: Touch-move: a piece of your own that you touch on purpose must be moved if it can move legally. Announcing an adjustment works only before touching, and only to straighten a piece.

displayText: Good players are gracious in defeat: shake hands, congratulate your opponent, and learn from the game.
text: Good players are gracious in defeat: shake hands, congratulate your opponent, and learn from the game.

displayText: Use the hand that moved the piece to press the clock as well.
text: Use the hand that moved the piece to press the clock as well.

displayText: The arbiter settles disputes. Pause the clock and ask for the arbiter instead of arguing with your opponent.
text: The arbiter settles disputes. Pause the clock and ask for the arbiter instead of arguing with your opponent.

displayText: Black's bishop on c4 covers f1, which the king has to pass over to castle kingside, so that side is closed. Queenside castling works: the king goes from e1 to c1.
text: Black's bishop on C four covers F one, which the king has to pass over to castle kingside, so that side is closed. Queenside castling works: the king goes from E one to C one.

displayText: Capturing en passant, from e5 to d6, removes the pawn on d5, and the white pawn on d6 now attacks the king on c7.
text: Capturing en passant, from E five to D six, removes the pawn on D five, and the white pawn on D six now attacks the king on C seven.

displayText: The king goes to g1 and the rook hops over to f1. On the other side the knight and queen still block the way, so only kingside castling is possible.
text: The king goes to G one and the rook hops over to F one. On the other side the knight and queen still block the way, so only kingside castling is possible.

displayText: Developing the knights and bishops and castling early gets your army ready and keeps your king safe.
text: Developing the knights and bishops and castling early gets your army ready and keeps your king safe.

displayText: The queen captures on f7. The bishop on c4 guards her, so the king cannot take, and the king has nowhere to go.
text: The queen captures on F seven. The bishop on C four guards her, so the king cannot take, and the king has nowhere to go.

displayText: The queen captures on f2, guarded by the bishop on c5, and it is checkmate. Taking with the bishop also mates, because then the queen guards f2.
text: The queen captures on F two, guarded by the bishop on C five, and it is checkmate. Taking with the bishop also mates, because then the queen guards F two.

displayText: The knight jumps to c7. It checks the king on e8 and attacks the queen on a8, and nothing can capture it.
text: The knight jumps to C seven. It checks the king on E eight and attacks the queen on A eight, and nothing can capture it.

displayText: The pawn moves to d5 and attacks both knights. Neither knight can capture it, and only one can move away, so White wins a knight for at most a pawn.
text: The pawn moves to D five and attacks both knights. Neither knight can capture it, and only one can move away, so White wins a knight for at most a pawn.

displayText: None. Any knight move would leave Black's king in check from the bishop on b5, and that is against the rules.
text: None. Any knight move would leave Black's king in check from the bishop on B five, and that is against the rules.

displayText: This is a relative pin, so every normal knight move is legal. Each one lets the bishop on g5 capture the queen on d8, though.
text: This is a relative pin, so every normal knight move is legal. Each one lets the bishop on G five capture the queen on D eight, though.

displayText: The rook moves to h6 and checks the king on d6. The king must leave the rank, and then the rook captures the queen on a6.
text: The rook moves to H six and checks the king on D six. The king must leave the rank, and then the rook captures the queen on A six.

displayText: The bishop moves to b3 and checks the king. Once the king steps off the diagonal, the bishop captures the rook on g8.
text: The bishop moves to B three and checks the king. Once the king steps off the diagonal, the bishop captures the rook on G eight.

displayText: The pawn steps from d3 to d4. That uncovers the bishop on b1, which now checks the king on h7, and the pawn attacks both the queen on c5 and the knight on e5. Black must answer the check, and whatever Black does, White wins the queen: if the queen blocks on c2, the bishop takes it with check.
text: The pawn steps from D three to D four. That uncovers the bishop on B one, which now checks the king on H seven, and the pawn attacks both the queen on C five and the knight on E five. Black must answer the check, and whatever Black does, White wins the queen: if the queen blocks on C two, the bishop takes it with check.

displayText: The knight jumps to f7 and checks the king on h8, and the bishop on b2 checks it too. Against a double check only the king can move, but g7 is guarded by the bishop and g8 and h7 hold Black's own pieces. Checkmate.
text: The knight jumps to F seven and checks the king on H eight, and the bishop on B two checks it too. Against a double check only the king can move, but G seven is guarded by the bishop and G eight and H seven hold Black's own pieces. Checkmate.

displayText: Two pieces guard d5: the pawn on c6, which captures diagonally forward onto d5, and the knight on f6. To win the knight on d5, White would first have to remove its guards.
text: Two pieces guard D five: the pawn on C six, which captures diagonally forward onto D five, and the knight on F six. To win the knight on D five, White would first have to remove its guards.

displayText: The bishop takes the knight on f6, and nothing can take it back. Now the bishop on d5 has lost its guard, and White's rook is ready to win it too.
text: The bishop takes the knight on F six, and nothing can take it back. Now the bishop on D five has lost its guard, and White's rook is ready to win it too.

displayText: The rook goes to b8 and checks along the last rank. The rook on a7 still guards e7, f7 and g7, so Black's king has no square left. Checkmate.
text: The rook goes to B eight and checks along the last rank. The rook on A seven still guards E seven, F seven and G seven, so Black's king has no square left. Checkmate.

displayText: The rook slides along the second rank to h2 and checks up the h-file. The rook on g1 guards the whole g-file, so the king cannot step sideways. The ladder works towards a side edge too.
text: The rook slides along the second rank to H two and checks up the h-file. The rook on G one guards the whole g-file, so the king cannot step sideways. The ladder works towards a side edge too.

displayText: The queen on e4 guards the e-file and the diagonal through f5 and g6, so the king can only go to f7, g5 or g7. All three are inside the box.
text: The queen on E four guards the e-file and the diagonal through F five and G six, so the king can only go to F seven, G five or G seven. All three are inside the box.

displayText: The queen checks along the a-file from a6 or a3. White's king guards b7 and b8, and the queen guards a7, so it is checkmate. A queen move to b6 would be a mistake: the king would not be in check but would have no legal move, which is stalemate.
text: The queen checks along the a-file from A six or A three. White's king guards B seven and B eight, and the queen guards A seven, so it is checkmate. A queen move to B six would be a mistake: the king would not be in check but would have no legal move, which is stalemate.

displayText: The rook checks along the last rank from a8. White's king on f6 covers e7, f7 and g7, and the rook covers e8 and g8. Checkmate.
text: The rook checks along the last rank from A eight. White's king on F six covers E seven, F seven and G seven, and the rook covers E eight and G eight. Checkmate.

displayText: The rook checks from b8 along the last rank. White's king on g6 covers g7 and h7, and the rook covers g8. Checkmate.
text: The rook checks from B eight along the last rank. White's king on G six covers G seven and H seven, and the rook covers G eight. Checkmate.

displayText: The knight jumps to e7 with check and attacks the queen on c6 too. Black must move the king, and then the knight captures the queen.
text: The knight jumps to E seven with check and attacks the queen on C six too. Black must move the king, and then the knight captures the queen.

displayText: The queen takes the bishop on g5, and nothing can take her back. The pawn on d5 is guarded by the queen and the knight, and the king guards f7.
text: The queen takes the bishop on G five, and nothing can take her back. The pawn on D five is guarded by the queen and the knight, and the king guards F seven.

displayText: Rook to d8 is check along the back rank. The black pawns on f7, g7 and h7 hem in their own king, and nothing can block the check or capture the rook.
text: Rook to D eight is check along the back rank. The black pawns on F seven, G seven and H seven hem in their own king, and nothing can block the check or capture the rook.

displayText: The queen moves to g7, right beside the king. White's king on f6 guards her, so the black king cannot take her, and she covers every square it could reach.
text: The queen moves to G seven, right beside the king. White's king on F six guards her, so the black king cannot take her, and she covers every square it could reach.

displayText: White castles queenside: the king goes to c1 and the rook to d1. The king is safer, and the rook joins the attack along the d-file.
text: White castles queenside: the king goes to C one and the rook to D one. The king is safer, and the rook joins the attack along the d-file.

displayText: The bishop moves to d8 and checks the king. The rook on d1 guards the bishop and covers d6 and d7, and Black's own pieces block the other squares.
text: The bishop moves to D eight and checks the king. The rook on D one guards the bishop and covers D six and D seven, and Black's own pieces block the other squares.

displayText: The knight takes the bishop on h4, and no black piece can reach h4. The knight on c6 is guarded by the pawn on b7, and the knight on e5 is guarded twice.
text: The knight takes the bishop on H four, and no black piece can reach H four. The knight on C six is guarded by the pawn on B seven, and the knight on E five is guarded twice.

displayText: The pawn moves to e5 and attacks both knights, on d6 and f6. No black piece can take the pawn, and no knight move gives check, so White wins a knight for at most a pawn.
text: The pawn moves to E five and attacks both knights, on D six and F six. No black piece can take the pawn, and no knight move gives check, so White wins a knight for at most a pawn.

displayText: The knight jumps to f7 and checks the king. The king's own rook and pawns fill every square around it, and nothing can capture the knight. This is called a smothered mate.
text: The knight jumps to F seven and checks the king. The king's own rook and pawns fill every square around it, and nothing can capture the knight. This is called a smothered mate.

displayText: The bishop on f5 and the pawn on b7 have no defender. The knight guards the rook and the pawn on a7, the pawn on b7 guards the knight, and the king guards f7, g7 and h7.
text: The bishop on F five and the pawn on B seven have no defender. The knight guards the rook and the pawn on A seven, the pawn on B seven guards the knight, and the king guards F seven, G seven and H seven.
